Tiny animals called tardigrades have survived open space.
In 2007 they rode outside a spacecraft, exposed to cold, vacuum and radiation. Some came back alive and even had babies.
Sharks are older than trees.
Sharks have been around for about 450 million years. The first true trees appeared roughly 385 million years ago.
The Greenland shark may live for around 400 years.
Scientists dated the eyes of one female to between about 270 and 500 years old, making it the longest-lived animal with a backbone known.
A mantis shrimp punches as fast as a small bullet leaves a gun.
Its club moves so quickly that the water boils into tiny bubbles, which pop and hit the prey a second time.
Octopuses can taste with their arms.
Their suckers have chemical sensors, so touching something tells them how it tastes.
Wombats leave cube-shaped droppings.
Their gut walls are stiff in some places and stretchy in others, which shapes the droppings into little cubes.
Crows remember human faces for years.
In a study in Seattle, crows scolded a mask worn by researchers who had caught them, and even young crows learned to do the same.
Elephants are among the very few mammals that cannot jump.
Their legs are built to carry great weight, so at least one foot always stays on the ground.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
Their wings swing in a figure-eight and can beat around 50 times a second.
Owls cannot move their eyes.
Their eyes are tube-shaped and fixed in place, so they turn their heads instead, up to about 270 degrees.
Axolotls can regrow legs, and even parts of their heart and brain.
This Mexican salamander rebuilds lost body parts without scars, and scientists study it to learn about healing.
One jellyfish can turn itself back into a baby.
When stressed, Turritopsis dohrnii can change from an adult back into its early polyp stage, which is why it is called the 'immortal jellyfish'.
Electric eels can give a shock of about 860 volts.
That is several times the power from a wall socket. They use it to stun prey and scare off attackers.
Cheetahs cannot roar. They purr.
Lions and tigers roar, but cheetahs chirp, hiss and purr like a big house cat.
Platypuses glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.
Scientists noticed it in 2020. No one is sure yet why their fur does this.
A blue whale's heart weighs about 180 kilograms.
Scientists who studied one found its heartbeat could slow to just two beats a minute during a dive.
Some kinds of bamboo can grow almost a metre in one day.
Bamboo is a grass, and its fastest species are among the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
The largest single flower in the world smells like rotting meat.
Rafflesia arnoldii can be about a metre across. The smell attracts the flies that carry its pollen.
A desert plant in Namibia lives more than 1,000 years with only two leaves.
Welwitschia's two leaves keep growing all its life, splitting into ribbons in the wind.
One of the heaviest living things is a forest that is really one tree.
Pando, in Utah, is about 47,000 aspen trunks all joined by one root system and sharing the same genes.
Babies are born with more bones than adults.
A newborn has around 270 to 300 bones. Many fuse together, leaving adults with 206.
Your body gives off a very faint glow.
A Japanese study in 2009 used special cameras to show humans glow slightly, about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see.
Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.
That is why whales can hear each other across huge distances in the ocean.
Diamonds can burn.
A diamond is pure carbon. Heated to around 700 °C or more in air, it burns away like coal.
One gram of gold can be hammered into a sheet about one square metre wide.
Gold is so soft and easy to shape that gold leaf can be thinner than a hair is wide.
Earth's inner core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun.
It is around 5,000 °C or more, but enormous pressure keeps it solid.
Earth is not a perfect ball.
Spinning makes it bulge at the equator, so it is about 43 km wider across the middle than from pole to pole.
The smell of rain has a name: petrichor.
Two Australian scientists named it in 1964. Much of the smell comes from geosmin, made by soil bacteria, and people can sniff out tiny amounts.
Only female mosquitoes bite.
They need protein from blood to make eggs. Males drink plant juice. The Aedes mosquito that spreads dengue bites mostly in the daytime.
Cats cannot taste sweet things.
They are missing a working gene for the sweet taste sensor, so sugar means nothing to them.
Helium was found on the Sun before it was found on Earth.
Scientists saw a strange yellow line in sunlight during an 1868 eclipse. Helium was only found on Earth in 1895.
Lightning is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
A bolt heats the air to around 30,000 °C for a split second, which makes the air explode outwards: that is thunder.
An ordinary puffy cloud can weigh about 500 tonnes.
The water is spread into tiny droplets over a huge space, so it floats on rising warm air.
Dust from the Sahara helps feed the Amazon rainforest.
Wind carries millions of tonnes of dust across the Atlantic each year, bringing phosphorus that the rainforest's plants need.
Water can boil and freeze at the same time.
At one exact low pressure and temperature, called the triple point, ice, water and vapour can all exist together.
Bananas are very slightly radioactive.
They contain potassium, and a tiny part of natural potassium is radioactive. You would need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold water.
It is called the Mpemba effect, after a Tanzanian student who noticed it in the 1960s. Scientists still argue about when and why it happens.
Voyager 1 is more than 24 billion kilometres from Earth.
Launched in 1977, it is the farthest human-made object. Its radio messages take almost a day to reach us.
The Moon is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm every year.
Scientists measure it by bouncing lasers off mirrors left on the Moon by astronauts.
Days on Earth are slowly getting longer.
The Moon's pull acts like a brake. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was only about 21 or 22 hours long.
Astronauts on the space station see about 16 sunrises every day.
The station circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes, at about 28,000 km per hour.
Sunsets on Mars are blue.
Mars dust scatters blue light forward towards the setting Sun, the opposite of what our air does.
Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Everest.
This volcano is about 22 km high and so wide that, standing on it, its slopes would disappear beyond the horizon.
Saturn's moon Titan has lakes and rain, but not of water.
It is so cold there that methane and ethane, which are gases on Earth, fall as rain and fill lakes.
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets.
On Venus the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.
Uranus spins on its side.
It is tilted about 98 degrees, probably after a huge crash long ago, so each pole gets about 42 years of sunlight and then 42 years of darkness.
Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system.
They reach about 2,000 km per hour, even though Neptune gets very little heat from the far-away Sun.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is shrinking.
In the 1800s this storm was wide enough to swallow about three Earths. Now it would fit just over one.
A teaspoon of a neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes.
These dead stars squeeze more than the mass of our Sun into a ball about 20 km wide.
One day on Mercury, sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 176 Earth days.
That is two of Mercury's years, because it spins slowly while racing around the Sun.
GPS satellites would get your location wrong without Einstein's ideas.
Their clocks tick about 38 microseconds a day faster than ours, because of speed and weaker gravity. Without fixing that, errors would grow by kilometres a day.
A single teaspoon of healthy soil can hold more living things than there are people on Earth.
Most are bacteria and fungi, which break down dead plants and keep soil fertile.
Some frogs freeze solid in winter and thaw back to life in spring.
The North American wood frog stops breathing and its heart stops. Sugar in its cells protects them from ice.
Pigeons can find their way home using the Earth's magnetic field.
They also use the Sun and smells, which is how racing pigeons return from hundreds of kilometres away.
Honey bees tell each other where flowers are by dancing.
A bee's 'waggle dance' shows the direction of food compared with the Sun and how far away it is.
Some bacteria can live inside nuclear reactors.
Deinococcus radiodurans survives radiation thousands of times stronger than would kill a person.
The coldest natural temperature measured on Earth was about minus 89 °C.
It was recorded at Vostok Station in Antarctica in 1983.
Starfish have no brain and no blood.
They move water through their bodies instead of blood, and have an eye at the tip of each arm.
Some trees warn each other about hungry insects.
Acacia trees being eaten by giraffes release a gas that makes nearby trees fill their leaves with bitter chemicals.
The human eye can see a candle flame from very far away on a clear dark night.
Lab tests suggest people can notice a few photons of light, and a flame might be seen from more than 2 km away.
